It's more complex and costly than plain CMOS, and still sensitive to static.

question: Which of the following digital logic families has the lowest power consumption?
explanation: CMOS draws almost no current except when switching, because in each stable state one of its complementary transistors is always off. Its static power consumption is extremely low, which is why it dominates battery-powered and large-scale ICs. ECL and TTL draw continuous current.

question: Why do CMOS digital integrated circuits have high immunity to noise on the input signal or power supply?
choices: The input switching threshold is about twice the power supply voltage
The input switching threshold is about half the power supply voltage
explanation: A CMOS input switches at about half the supply voltage. A noise spike on the input would need to be nearly half the supply voltage (e.g., 2.5 V on a 5 V supply) to cause a false transition. That wide noise margin is why CMOS is highly immune to noise.

question: What best describes a pull-up or pull-down resistor?
choices: A resistor in a keying circuit used to reduce key clicks
A resistor connected to the positive or negative supply used to establish a voltage when an input or output is an open circuit
A resistor that ensures that an oscillator frequency does not drift
A resistor connected to an op-amp output that prevents signals from exceeding the power supply voltage
explanation: A pull-up (to the positive supply) or pull-down (to ground) resistor sets a defined logic level on an input or output that would otherwise float when nothing is actively driving it, such as an open switch or an open-collector output. A floating input can pick up noise and switch randomly.

question: In Figure E6-3, which is the schematic symbol for a NAND gate?
explanation: Symbol 2. A NAND gate is drawn as an AND gate body (flat back, round front) with a small circle (inversion bubble) at the output. Symbol 1 is AND, 3 is OR, 4 is NOR and 5 is an inverter.

question: What is used to design the configuration of a field-programmable gate array (FPGA)?
explanation: FPGAs are configured using a hardware description language (HDL) such as VHDL or Verilog. The designer describes the logic in text, and software converts it into a configuration that connects the FPGA's internal logic blocks. Karnaugh maps are only used for simplifying small logic functions by hand.

question: In Figure E6-3, which is the schematic symbol for a NOR gate?
explanation: Symbol 4. A NOR gate is drawn as an OR gate body (curved back, pointed front) with an inversion bubble at the output. Symbol 3 without the bubble is OR, and symbol 2 is NAND.

question: In Figure E6-3, which is the schematic symbol for the NOT operation (inversion)?
explanation: Symbol 5. The NOT operation (inverter) is shown as a triangle (a buffer) with an inversion bubble at the output. It has only one input and one output.

question: What is piezoelectricity?
choices: The ability of materials to generate electromagnetic waves of a certain frequency when voltage is applied
A characteristic of materials that have an index of refraction which depends on the polarization of the electromagnetic wave passing through it
A characteristic of materials that generate a voltage when stressed and that flex when a voltage is applied
The ability of materials to generate voltage when an electromagnetic wave of a certain frequency is applied
explanation: Piezoelectricity is the property of certain crystals (quartz, some ceramics) to generate a voltage when mechanically stressed, and to flex or deform when a voltage is applied. In a quartz crystal, this couples a precise mechanical vibration to the electrical circuit, which is what makes crystals such stable frequency references.

question: What is the equivalent circuit of a quartz crystal?
choices: Series RLC in parallel with a shunt C representing electrode and stray capacitance
Parallel RLC, where C is the parallel combination of resonance capacitance of the crystal and electrode and stray capacitance
Series RLC, where C is the parallel combination of resonance capacitance of the crystal and electrode and stray capacitance
Parallel RLC, where C is the series combination of resonance capacitance of the crystal and electrode and stray capacitance
explanation: The mechanical vibration of the crystal behaves like a series RLC circuit (motional L, C and R). In parallel with it is the shunt capacitance C0 formed by the electrodes and holder. That's why a crystal has two resonances: a series resonance and a slightly higher parallel resonance.

question: Which of the following is an aspect of the piezoelectric effect?
choices: Mechanical deformation of material due to the application of a voltage
Mechanical deformation of material due to the application of a magnetic field
Generation of electrical energy in the presence of light
Increased conductivity in the presence of light
explanation: The piezoelectric effect works both ways: mechanical stress produces a voltage, and an applied voltage produces mechanical deformation. The correct choice describes the second effect. Deformation by a magnetic field is magnetostriction, and the light-related choices describe photovoltaic and photoconductive effects.

question: Why are cores of inductors and transformers sometimes constructed of thin layers?
choices: To reduce power loss from eddy currents in the core
To increase the cutoff frequency by reducing capacitance
To save cost by reducing the amount of magnetic material
explanation: The changing magnetic field in a transformer core also induces currents in the core itself (eddy currents), which heat it and waste power. Building the core from thin, insulated laminations breaks up the paths these currents can take, greatly reducing eddy current losses. At RF, ferrite or powdered iron cores serve the same purpose.

question: How do ferrite and powdered iron compare for use in an inductor core?
choices: Ferrite cores generally have lower initial permeability
Ferrite cores generally have better temperature stability
Ferrite cores generally require fewer turns to produce a given inductance value
Ferrite cores are easier to use with surface-mount technology
explanation: Ferrite has much higher permeability than powdered iron, so a ferrite core needs fewer turns to produce a given inductance. Powdered iron has lower permeability but better temperature stability and lower loss at higher RF frequencies, so it's preferred for tuned circuits. Ferrite is preferred for chokes and broadband transformers.

question: What core material property determines the inductance of an inductor?
explanation: Permeability is the ability of a material to concentrate magnetic flux. A core with permeability µ multiplies the inductance of an air-core coil by roughly µ. Permittivity is the equivalent property for electric fields (capacitors).

question: Which of the following materials has the highest temperature stability of its magnetic characteristics?
explanation: Of the choices, powdered iron has the best temperature stability of its magnetic properties, so it's used in tuned circuits and oscillators where inductance must not drift. Ferrite has higher permeability but it changes more with temperature. Brass and aluminum aren't magnetic.

question: What devices are commonly used as VHF and UHF parasitic suppressors at the input and output terminals of a transistor HF amplifier?
explanation: Ferrite beads slipped over the leads of transistors act as small, lossy inductors. They have little effect at HF but absorb energy at VHF and UHF, where transistors might otherwise break into parasitic oscillation, damping it out.

question: What is a primary advantage of using a toroidal core instead of a solenoidal core in an inductor?
choices: Toroidal cores confine most of the magnetic field within the core material
Toroidal cores make it easier to couple the magnetic energy into other components
Toroidal cores have lower Q characteristics
explanation: In a toroid, the magnetic field is almost entirely confined within the ring-shaped core, so it doesn't couple into nearby components or pick up stray fields. This allows compact layouts without shielding and reduces unwanted coupling. A solenoid (straight coil) has a large external field.

question: Which type of core material decreases inductance when inserted into a coil?
explanation: Brass is a good conductor but not magnetic. The coil's magnetic field induces eddy currents in a brass slug, which create an opposing field that reduces the coil's inductance. Ferrite or powdered iron slugs increase inductance. (Aluminum also reduces inductance, but brass is the expected answer.)

question: What causes inductor saturation?
choices: Operation at too high a frequency
Selecting a core with low permeability
Selecting a core with excessive permittivity
explanation: Every magnetic core material can only hold so much magnetic flux. When the current (and so the flux) is too high, the core saturates: further current produces little additional flux, so the inductance drops dramatically. In power circuits this can cause overheating, and in RF circuits distortion and harmonics.

question: Why is gallium arsenide (GaAs) useful for semiconductor devices operating at UHF and higher frequencies?
explanation: Gallium arsenide has higher electron mobility than silicon, so electrons move through the device faster and it can amplify at UHF and microwave frequencies with lower noise. The distractors (higher noise figures, lower transconductance) would be disadvantages.

question: Which of the following device packages is a through-hole type?
explanation: DIP (dual in-line package) is a through-hole package: its pins go through holes in the circuit board and are soldered on the other side. PLCC, BGA and SOT are surface-mount packages, soldered directly to pads on the board surface.

question: Which of the following materials supports the highest frequency of operation when used in MMICs?
explanation: Gallium nitride (GaN) supports the highest frequencies of these choices and also handles high power and voltage. GaN MMICs are used for microwave power amplifiers. Silicon nitride and silicon dioxide are insulators used in IC manufacturing, not semiconductor materials.

question: Which is the most common input and output impedance of MMICs?
explanation: Most MMICs are designed with 50 Ω input and output impedances, the standard impedance of RF systems and coaxial cable. That lets them be cascaded and connected to other RF parts without matching networks.

question: Which of the following noise figure values is typical of a low-noise UHF preamplifier?
explanation: Good low-noise UHF preamplifiers (typically GaAs FETs or PHEMTs) have noise figures around 0.5 dB, adding very little noise. The distractors have impossible values (negative noise figure) or the wrong units (dBm is a power level).

question: What characteristics of MMICs make them a popular choice for VHF through microwave circuits?
choices: The ability to retrieve information from a single signal, even in the presence of other strong signals
Extremely high Q factor and high stability over a wide temperature range
Nearly infinite gain, very high input impedance, and very low output impedance
Controlled gain, low noise figure, and constant input and output impedance over the specified frequency range
explanation: MMICs (monolithic microwave integrated circuits) are popular because they offer controlled gain, a low noise figure and constant input and output impedance (usually 50 Ω) over their specified frequency range, with few external parts. Choice C describes an op-amp.

question: What type of transmission line is often used for connections to MMICs?
explanation: MMICs are usually connected with microstrip: a copper trace of a specific width on a circuit board, over a ground plane on the other side. The trace width sets the characteristic impedance (usually 50 Ω), giving a controlled-impedance line that's easy to manufacture.

question: How is power supplied to the most common type of MMIC?
choices: Through a capacitor and RF choke connected to the amplifier input lead
Through a resistor and/or RF choke connected to the amplifier output lead
Directly to the bias voltage (Vcc) lead
explanation: The most common MMICs have their DC supply applied through the output lead. A resistor and/or RF choke feeds DC to the output pin while keeping RF from escaping into the power supply, and coupling capacitors block the DC from the input and output connections.

question: Which of the following component package types have the least parasitic effects at frequencies above the HF range?
explanation: Surface-mount components have little or no lead length, so their parasitic inductance and capacitance are much smaller than those of leaded packages like TO-220, axial or radial parts. This makes them the best choice above HF.

question: What advantage does surface-mount technology offer at RF compared to using through-hole components?
choices: Components have less parasitic inductance and capacitance
explanation: All three. Surface-mount parts are smaller, allowing a smaller circuit area and shorter traces between components, and they have less parasitic inductance and capacitance. All of this improves RF performance.

question: What is a characteristic of DIP packaging used for integrated circuits?
choices: Extremely low stray capacitance (dielectrically isolated package)
Extremely high resistance between pins (doubly insulated package)
Two chips in each package (dual in package)
Two rows of connecting pins on opposite sides of package (dual in-line package)
explanation: DIP stands for dual in-line package: two parallel rows of pins, one on each long side of the package, with 0.1-inch (2.54 mm) pin spacing.

question: Why are DIP through-hole package ICs not typically used at UHF and higher frequencies?
choices: Epoxy coating is conductive above 300 MHz
Unsuitable for combining analog and digital signals
explanation: The leads of a DIP package are relatively long (several millimeters) and have inductance that becomes significant at UHF and above, where it adds reactance and unwanted coupling. Surface-mount packages with minimal leads are used instead.

question: What absorbs the energy from light falling on a photovoltaic cell?
explanation: In a photovoltaic cell, the energy of light (photons) is absorbed by electrons in the semiconductor, freeing them from their atoms. The electric field at the P-N junction sweeps these freed electrons across, producing a current. Photons are what's absorbed, electrons are what absorb them.

question: What happens to photoconductive material when light shines on it?
explanation: Light striking a photoconductive material frees additional charge carriers (electrons and holes), so its resistance decreases. A cadmium sulfide photocell might measure megohms in darkness and only a few hundred ohms in bright light.

question: What is the most common configuration of an optoisolator or optocoupler?
explanation: The most common optoisolator contains an LED and a phototransistor sealed in one package. The input current lights the LED, and the light turns on the phototransistor. The signal crosses a gap with only light, providing electrical isolation up to several thousand volts.

question: What is the photovoltaic effect?
choices: The conversion of voltage to current when exposed to light
The conversion of light to electrical energy
The effect that causes a photodiode to emit light when a voltage is applied
The effect that causes a phototransistor’s beta to decrease when exposed to light
explanation: The photovoltaic effect is the direct conversion of light into electrical energy. It's how solar cells work: light frees electrons at a P-N junction, producing a voltage and a current that can power a load.

question: Which of the following describes an optical shaft encoder?
choices: A device that detects rotation by interrupting a light source with a patterned wheel
A device that measures the strength of a beam of light using analog-to-digital conversion
An optical computing device in which light is coupled between devices by fiber optics
A device for generating RTTY signals by means of a rotating light source
explanation: An optical shaft encoder has a disk with a pattern of slots or marks attached to a shaft. As the shaft turns, the pattern interrupts a light beam, and a photodetector produces pulses indicating the rotation and direction. Many transceivers use one for the tuning knob.

question: Which of these materials is most commonly used to create photoconductive devices?
explanation: Photoconductive devices are most commonly made of crystalline semiconductors such as cadmium sulfide, cadmium selenide, or silicon and germanium. In these materials light frees charge carriers and lowers resistance.

question: What is a solid-state relay?
choices: A relay that uses transistors to drive the relay coil
A device that uses semiconductors to implement the functions of an electromechanical relay
A mechanical relay that latches in the on or off state each time it is pulsed
A semiconductor switch that uses a monostable multivibrator circuit
explanation: A solid-state relay uses semiconductors (typically an optoisolator driving a triac, SCR or MOSFETs) to perform the switching function of an electromechanical relay, with no moving parts. It switches silently, doesn't wear out and doesn't produce contact bounce or arcing.

question: Why are optoisolators often used in conjunction with solid-state circuits that control 120 VAC circuits?
choices: Optoisolators provide a low-impedance link between a control circuit and a power circuit
Optoisolators provide impedance matching between the control circuit and power circuit
Optoisolators provide an electrical isolation between a control circuit and the circuit being switched
Optoisolators eliminate the effects of reflected light in the control circuit
explanation: Optoisolators provide electrical isolation between the low-voltage control circuit and the circuit being switched, which may be at 120 VAC line potential. Only light crosses between them, protecting both the control circuit and the person operating it from the line voltage.

question: What is the efficiency of a photovoltaic cell?
choices: The output RF power divided by the input DC power
The output in lumens divided by the input power in watts
The open-circuit voltage divided by the short-circuit current under full illumination
The relative fraction of light that is converted to current
explanation: The efficiency of a photovoltaic cell is the fraction of the light energy falling on it that is converted to electrical energy. Typical silicon solar cells are about 15-22% efficient.

question: What is the most common material used in power-generating photovoltaic cells?
explanation: Silicon is by far the most common material for power-generating photovoltaic (solar) cells, as monocrystalline, polycrystalline or amorphous silicon. It's abundant, well understood and reasonably efficient.

question: What is the approximate open-circuit voltage produced by a fully illuminated silicon photovoltaic cell?
explanation: A fully illuminated silicon photovoltaic cell produces about 0.5 V open-circuit (up to about 0.6 V). Solar panels connect many cells in series to reach useful voltages: a nominal '12 V' panel has 36 cells, giving about 18-21 V open-circuit.

question: Which circuit is bistable?
explanation: A flip-flop is bistable: it has two stable states and stays in whichever one it's set to until it gets an input telling it to change. That's why a flip-flop can store one bit. Gates (AND, OR) have no memory; their outputs simply follow the inputs.

question: What is the function of a decade counter?
choices: It produces one output pulse for every 10 input pulses
It decodes a decimal number for display on a seven-segment LED display
It produces 10 output pulses for every input pulse
It decodes a binary number for display on a seven-segment LED display
explanation: A decade counter counts input pulses from 0 to 9 and then resets, producing one output pulse for every 10 input pulses. This divides the frequency by 10. Frequency counters and dividers are built from chains of decade counters.

question: Which of the following can divide the frequency of a pulse train by 2?
explanation: A toggle (T) or J-K flip-flop set to toggle changes state on every input pulse, so its output completes one full cycle for every two input pulses: it divides the frequency by 2. Chaining flip-flops divides by 4, 8, 16, and so on.

question: How many flip-flops are required to divide a signal frequency by 16?
explanation: Each flip-flop divides by 2, so n flip-flops divide by 2^n. 16 = 2^4, so 4 flip-flops are needed: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16.

question: Which of the following circuits continuously alternates between two states without an external clock signal?
explanation: An astable multivibrator has no stable state: it keeps switching back and forth between its two states on its own, producing a square wave with no external clock. A 555 timer in astable mode is a common example. A monostable has one stable state and flip-flops have two.

question: What is a characteristic of a monostable multivibrator?
choices: It switches temporarily to an alternate state for a set time
It produces a continuous square wave
It stores one bit of data
It maintains a constant output voltage, regardless of variations in the input voltage
explanation: A monostable multivibrator ('one-shot') has one stable state. When triggered, it switches to its other state for a fixed time set by an RC time constant, then returns on its own. It's used to generate pulses of a set length, for example for debouncing or timing.

question: What logical operation does a NAND gate perform?
choices: It produces a 0 at its output only if all inputs are 0
It produces a 1 at its output only if all inputs are 1
It produces a 0 at its output if some but not all inputs are 1
It produces a 0 at its output only if all inputs are 1
explanation: A NAND gate (NOT-AND) produces a 0 only if all of its inputs are 1; any other combination gives a 1. It's the inverse of an AND gate, which produces a 1 only when all inputs are 1.

question: What logical operation does an OR gate perform?
choices: It produces a 1 at its output if any input is 1
It produces a 0 at its output if all inputs are 1
It produces a 0 at its output if some but not all inputs are 1
It produces a 1 at its output if all inputs are 0
explanation: An OR gate produces a 1 at its output if any input (one or more) is 1. The output is 0 only when all inputs are 0.

question: What logical operation is performed by a two-input exclusive NOR gate?
choices: It produces a 0 at its output only if all inputs are 0
It produces a 1 at its output only if all inputs are 1
It produces a 0 at its output if one and only one of its inputs is 1
It produces a 1 at its output if one and only one input is 1
explanation: A two-input XNOR gate outputs 1 when both inputs are the same (both 0 or both 1) and 0 when they differ, i.e., when one and only one input is 1. It's an equality detector. XOR is the opposite: 1 when exactly one input is 1.

question: What is a truth table?
choices: A list of inputs and corresponding outputs for an op-amp
A list of inputs and corresponding outputs for a digital device
A diagram showing logic states when the digital gate output is true
A table of logic symbols that indicate the logic states of an op-amp
explanation: A truth table lists every possible combination of inputs to a digital device together with the resulting output. It completely describes a logic function; a two-input gate has 4 rows, a three-input gate has 8.

question: What does “positive logic” mean in reference to logic devices?
choices: The logic devices have high noise immunity
High voltage represents a 1, low voltage a 0
The logic circuit is in the “true” condition
1s and 0s are defined as different positive voltage levels
explanation: In positive logic, the higher voltage represents a 1 (true) and the lower voltage a 0 (false). Negative logic reverses this. Most modern logic families use positive logic, e.g., about 5 V or 3.3 V for 1 and 0 V for 0.

question: For what portion of the signal cycle does each active element in a push-pull, Class AB amplifier conduct?
choices: More than 180 degrees but less than 360 degrees
explanation: In Class AB push-pull, each device is biased slightly on, so it conducts for more than half the cycle (180°) but less than the full cycle (360°). The overlap near the zero crossing eliminates the crossover distortion of Class B while keeping much better efficiency than Class A (360°).

question: What is a Class D amplifier?
choices: An amplifier that uses switching technology to achieve high efficiency
A low power amplifier that uses a differential amplifier for improved linearity
An amplifier that uses drift-mode FETs for high efficiency
An amplifier biased to be relatively free from distortion
explanation: A Class D amplifier uses its active devices as switches that are either fully on or fully off, never in between, and uses pulse-width modulation or similar switching schemes. Because a switch dissipates almost no power in either state, efficiency can exceed 90%.

question: What circuit is required at the output of an RF switching amplifier?
choices: A filter to remove harmonic content
A high-pass filter to compensate for low gain at low frequencies
A matched load resistor to prevent damage by switching transients
A temperature compensating load resistor to improve linearity
explanation: A switching amplifier's output is essentially a square wave, rich in harmonics. A low-pass filter at the output removes the harmonic content, leaving a clean sine wave at the operating frequency to send to the antenna.

question: What is the operating point of a Class A common emitter amplifier?
choices: Approximately halfway between saturation and cutoff
Approximately halfway between the emitter voltage and the base voltage
At a point where the bias resistor equals the load resistor
At a point where the load line intersects the zero bias current curve
explanation: A Class A amplifier is biased so the operating point sits about halfway between saturation (fully on) and cutoff (fully off). The output can then swing equally in both directions, amplifying the whole signal with minimal distortion. The cost is low efficiency (at most 25-50%).

question: What can be done to prevent unwanted oscillations in an RF power amplifier?
choices: Tune the stage for minimum loading
Tune both the input and output for maximum power
Install parasitic suppressors and/or neutralize the stage
Use a phase inverter in the output filter
explanation: Unwanted oscillations are prevented with parasitic suppressors (small resistor-inductor combinations or ferrite beads that absorb VHF energy in the leads) and by neutralization (feeding back a small signal out of phase to cancel the internal feedback through the device's capacitance).

question: What is a characteristic of a grounded-grid amplifier?
explanation: In a grounded-grid amplifier the input signal is applied to the cathode, which carries the full plate current, so the input impedance is low (typically 50-100 Ω). This makes it easy to drive directly from a transceiver, and it is inherently stable, but its power gain is relatively low.

question: Which of the following is the likely result of using a Class C amplifier to amplify a single-sideband phone signal?
explanation: Class C amplifiers conduct for less than 180° of the cycle and are very nonlinear. SSB needs a linear amplifier because its amplitude varies with the voice. A Class C amplifier would distort the SSB envelope, creating intermodulation products that make the signal wider than it should be (splatter).

question: Why are switching amplifiers more efficient than linear amplifiers?
choices: Switching amplifiers operate at higher voltages
The switching device is at saturation or cutoff most of the time
Linear amplifiers have high gain resulting in higher harmonic content
explanation: In a switching amplifier the device is either saturated (fully on: high current but almost no voltage across it) or cut off (no current). Power dissipated = voltage × current, which is near zero in both states. A linear amplifier's device has substantial voltage and current at the same time, wasting power as heat.

question: What is characteristic of an emitter follower (or common collector) amplifier?
choices: Low input impedance and phase inversion from input to output
Acts as an OR circuit if one input is grounded
explanation: In an emitter follower (common collector), the output taken from the emitter follows the input voltage at the base, in phase and with slightly less than unity voltage gain. It has high input impedance and low output impedance, so it's used as a buffer or impedance transformer.

question: In Figure E7-1, what is the purpose of R1 and R2?
explanation: R1 (from the supply to the base) and R2 (from the base to ground) form a voltage divider that sets the base at a fixed DC voltage, the transistor's bias point. Divider bias is stable because it doesn't depend strongly on the transistor's beta.

question: In Figure E7-1, what is the purpose of R3?
explanation: R3 in the emitter provides self bias (emitter degeneration): if the collector current rises, the voltage across R3 rises, which reduces the base-emitter voltage and pulls the current back down. This stabilizes the operating point against temperature and transistor variation. C3 bypasses R3 for AC so it doesn't reduce the signal gain.

question: What type of amplifier circuit is shown in Figure E7-1?
explanation: The input goes into the base and the output is taken from the collector, while the emitter is common to both (connected to ground through R3, bypassed by C3). That's a common-emitter amplifier, which gives both voltage and current gain with 180° phase inversion.

question: How are the capacitors and inductors of a low-pass filter Pi-network arranged between the network’s input and output?
choices: Two inductors are in series between the input and output, and a capacitor is connected between the two inductors and ground
Two capacitors are in series between the input and output, and an inductor is connected between the two capacitors and ground
An inductor is connected between the input and ground, another inductor is connected between the output and ground, and a capacitor is connected between the input and output
A capacitor is connected between the input and ground, another capacitor is connected between the output and ground, and an inductor is connected between the input and output
explanation: A low-pass Pi-network has a capacitor from the input to ground, an inductor in series between the input and output, and another capacitor from the output to ground: it looks like the Greek letter π. The series inductor blocks high frequencies and the shunt capacitors short them to ground, so low frequencies pass.

question: What is the frequency response of a T-network with series capacitors and a shunt inductor?
explanation: The series capacitors pass high frequencies but block low ones (XC is high at low frequencies), and the shunt inductor shorts low frequencies to ground (XL is low at low frequencies). Both favor high frequencies, so it is a high-pass filter.

question: What is the purpose of adding an inductor to a Pi-network to create a Pi-L-network?
explanation: A Pi-L network adds a series inductor at the output of a Pi-network, forming a second low-pass section. The extra section provides greater harmonic suppression than a Pi-network alone, which is why it's common in tube amplifier output circuits.

question: How does an impedance-matching circuit transform a complex impedance to a resistive impedance?
choices: It introduces negative resistance to cancel the resistive part of impedance
It introduces transconductance to cancel the reactive part of impedance
It cancels the reactive part of the impedance and changes the resistive part to the desired value
Reactive currents are dissipated in matched resistances
explanation: An impedance-matching network cancels the reactive part of the load (adding equal and opposite reactance) and transforms the remaining resistance to the desired value (usually 50 Ω). It uses only reactive components, so ideally no power is lost.

question: Which filter type has ripple in the passband and a sharp cutoff?
explanation: A Chebyshev filter has ripple in the passband but a sharper cutoff than a Butterworth filter with the same number of components. A Butterworth filter has a maximally flat passband but a more gradual rolloff.

question: What are the characteristics of an elliptical filter?
choices: Gradual passband rolloff with minimal stop-band ripple
Extremely flat response over its pass band with gradually rounded stop-band corners
Extremely sharp cutoff with one or more notches in the stop band
Gradual passband rolloff with extreme stop-band ripple
explanation: An elliptic (Cauer) filter has an extremely sharp cutoff, with one or more notches (points of very high attenuation) in the stop band. It has ripple in both the passband and stop band. For a given number of components, it gives the steepest transition of any filter type.

question: Which describes a Pi-L network?
choices: A Pi-network with an additional output series inductor
A network with only three discrete parts
A matching network in which all components are isolated from ground
explanation: A Pi-L network is a Pi-network with an additional series inductor at the output (the 'L' section). It provides better harmonic suppression and matching range than a plain Pi-network.

question: Which of the following is most frequently used as a band-pass or notch filter in VHF and UHF transceivers?
explanation: Helical filters are made from coils inside shielded cavities, acting as high-Q resonators in a compact size. They're widely used as band-pass (and notch) filters in VHF and UHF transceivers. Sallen-Key filters are audio op-amp filters, and swinging chokes are used in power supplies.

question: What is a crystal lattice filter?
choices: A power supply filter made with interlaced quartz crystals
An audio filter made with four quartz crystals that resonate at 1 kHz intervals
A filter using lattice-shaped quartz crystals for high-Q performance
A filter for low-level signals made using quartz crystals
explanation: A crystal lattice filter uses several quartz crystals in a lattice or ladder circuit to create a very sharp, narrow filter, typically in a receiver's or transmitter's IF stage. It's used with low-level signals because the crystals can't handle much power.

question: Which of the following filters is used in a 2-meter band repeater duplexer?
explanation: A repeater duplexer uses cavity filters: large high-Q resonant cavities that pass the transmit frequency to the antenna while rejecting the receive frequency, and vice versa. On 2 meters the input and output are only 600 kHz apart, so very high Q (sharp filtering) is needed.

question: Which of the following measures a filter’s ability to reject signals in adjacent channels?
explanation: Shape factor is the ratio of a filter's bandwidth at a high attenuation level (e.g., −60 dB) to its bandwidth at a low attenuation level (e.g., −6 dB). The closer to 1, the steeper the filter skirts and the better it rejects signals in adjacent channels. A 2.4 kHz SSB filter with a shape factor of 1.5 is 3.6 kHz wide at −60 dB.

question: How does a linear electronic voltage regulator work?
choices: It has a ramp voltage as its output
It eliminates the need for a pass transistor
The control element duty cycle is proportional to the line or load conditions
The conduction of a control element is varied to maintain a constant output voltage
explanation: A linear regulator varies the conduction of a control element (usually a series pass transistor) continuously, like an automatically adjusted resistor, to maintain a constant output voltage as the input voltage or load changes. The excess voltage is dropped across the control element and dissipated as heat.

question: How does a switchmode voltage regulator work?
choices: By alternating the output between positive and negative voltages
By varying the duty cycle of pulses input to a filter
By varying the conductivity of a pass element
By switching between two Zener diode reference voltages
explanation: A switchmode regulator switches a transistor fully on and off rapidly and varies the duty cycle (the fraction of time it's on). The pulses are smoothed by an LC filter; the average output voltage depends on the duty cycle. Since the switch is always fully on or off, little power is wasted.

question: What device is used as a stable voltage reference?
explanation: A Zener diode maintains a nearly constant voltage in reverse breakdown, making it a simple, stable voltage reference. Voltage regulators compare their output to a Zener or similar reference (like a bandgap reference) to keep the output constant.

question: Which of the following describes a three-terminal voltage regulator?
explanation: A three-terminal regulator (like the 78xx or LM317 series) has input, output and ground or adjust terminals and is a series regulator: the pass transistor inside is in series between input and output. It includes the reference, error amplifier and protection circuits in one package.

question: Which of the following types of linear voltage regulator operates by loading the unregulated voltage source?
explanation: A shunt regulator is connected in parallel with the load and draws more or less current so that the total current through a series resistor keeps the output voltage constant. It works by loading the unregulated source: a Zener diode with a series resistor is the simplest example. It wastes power even with no load.

question: What is the purpose of Q1 in the circuit shown in Figure E7-2?
choices: It provides negative feedback to improve regulation
It provides a constant load for the voltage source
It controls the current to keep the output voltage constant
It provides regulation by switching or “chopping” the input DC voltage
explanation: Q1 is the series pass transistor. Its base is held at a fixed voltage by the Zener diode D1, and as an emitter follower the output is one diode drop (0.6 V) below the Zener voltage. Q1 automatically controls the current to keep the output voltage constant as the load changes.

question: What is the purpose of C2 in the circuit shown in Figure E7-2?
choices: It bypasses rectifier output ripple around D1
It is a brute force filter for the output
To provide fixed DC bias for Q1
explanation: C2 is in parallel with the Zener diode D1. It bypasses rectifier ripple (and noise) around D1, keeping the reference voltage at Q1's base smooth, so the regulated output is also smooth.

question: What type of circuit is shown in Figure E7-2?
explanation: Figure E7-2 is a linear voltage regulator: the Zener diode D1 sets a reference voltage, R1 supplies current to it, and Q1 is a series pass transistor that continuously varies its conduction to hold the output at about 12 V. Nothing switches on and off, so it's linear.

question: How is battery operating time calculated?
choices: Average current divided by capacity in amp-hours
Average current divided by internal resistance
Capacity in amp-hours divided by average current
Internal resistance divided by average current
explanation: Operating time = capacity in amp-hours ÷ average current in amps. A 100 Ah battery supplying an average of 5 A lasts about 100 / 5 = 20 hours (in practice less, since capacity drops at high currents and you shouldn't fully discharge most batteries).

question: Why is a switching type power supply less expensive and lighter than an equivalent linear power supply?
choices: The inverter design does not require an output filter circuit
The control circuitry uses less current, therefore smaller heat sinks are required
The high frequency inverter design uses much smaller transformers and filter components for an equivalent power output
It recovers power from the unused portion of the AC cycle, thus using fewer components
explanation: A switching supply converts the power at a high frequency (tens to hundreds of kHz) rather than 60 Hz. Transformer and filter capacitor size drops dramatically with frequency, so a switching supply's transformer and filters are much smaller and lighter, and cheaper than the heavy iron-core transformer and large capacitors of a linear supply.

question: What is the purpose of an inverter connected to a solar panel output?
choices: Reduce AC ripple on the output
Maintain voltage with varying illumination levels
Prevent discharge when panel is not illuminated
Convert the panel’s output from DC to AC
explanation: A solar panel produces DC. An inverter converts that DC to AC so it can run standard AC appliances or feed power into the utility grid. Maintaining voltage and preventing discharge are the jobs of a charge controller and blocking diode.

question: What is the dropout voltage of a linear voltage regulator?
choices: Minimum input voltage for rated power dissipation
Maximum output voltage drop when the input voltage is varied over its specified range
Minimum input-to-output voltage required to maintain regulation
Maximum that the output voltage may decrease at rated load
explanation: Dropout voltage is the minimum difference between input and output voltage a linear regulator needs to keep regulating. A standard regulator might need 2-3 V; a low-dropout (LDO) regulator only 0.1-0.5 V. If the input falls below output + dropout voltage, the output falls with it.

question: Which of the following calculates power dissipated by a series linear voltage regulator?
choices: Input voltage multiplied by input current
Input voltage divided by output current
Voltage difference from input to output multiplied by output current
Output voltage multiplied by output current
explanation: The pass element drops the difference between input and output voltage while carrying the full output current, so P = (Vin − Vout) × Iout. Example: 18 V in, 13.8 V out at 10 A dissipates 4.2 × 10 = 42 W, which the heat sink must remove.

question: What is the purpose of connecting equal-value resistors across power supply filter capacitors connected in series?
choices: Equalize the voltage across each capacitor
Discharge the capacitors when voltage is removed
Provide a minimum load on the supply
explanation: All three. Equal resistors across series capacitors (1) force the voltage to divide equally, since leakage currents differ and could put too much voltage on one capacitor; (2) act as bleeder resistors that discharge the capacitors when power is removed, for safety; and (3) provide a minimum load that improves the supply's voltage regulation.

question: What is the purpose of a step-start circuit in a high-voltage power supply?
choices: To provide a dual-voltage output for reduced power applications
To compensate for variations of the incoming line voltage
To prevent arcing across the input power switch or relay contacts
To allow the filter capacitors to charge gradually
explanation: When a high-voltage supply is switched on, the discharged filter capacitors act like a short circuit and draw a huge inrush current. A step-start circuit first applies power through a resistor that limits the current while the capacitors charge gradually, then shorts the resistor out with a relay.

question: Which of the following can be used to generate FM phone signals?
choices: Balanced modulation of the audio amplifier
Reactance modulation of a local oscillator
Reactance modulation of the final amplifier
Balanced modulation of a local oscillator
explanation: FM can be generated by reactance modulation of an oscillator: a varactor diode or reactance tube is connected to the oscillator's tuned circuit, and the audio varies its reactance, varying the oscillator frequency. Modulating the final amplifier would produce AM or PM effects, not true FM.

question: What is the function of a reactance modulator?
choices: Produce PM or FM signals by varying a resistance
Produce AM signals by varying an inductance
Produce AM signals by varying a resistance
Produce PM or FM signals by varying a capacitance
explanation: A reactance modulator varies a capacitance (or reactance) in step with the audio, producing FM (if applied to the oscillator) or PM (if applied to a later stage). A varactor diode is the usual variable capacitance.

question: What is a frequency discriminator?
choices: A circuit for filtering closely adjacent signals
A circuit for detecting FM signals
explanation: A frequency discriminator detects FM: it converts frequency deviations into voltage changes, recovering the audio. Other FM detectors include the ratio detector, quadrature detector and PLL detector.

question: What is one way to produce a single-sideband phone signal?
choices: Use a balanced modulator followed by a filter
Use a reactance modulator followed by a mixer
Use a loop modulator followed by a mixer
Use a product detector with a DSB signal
explanation: A balanced modulator produces a double-sideband signal with the carrier suppressed. A sharp crystal filter then removes the unwanted sideband, leaving a single sideband. This 'filter method' is the classic SSB generator; the 'phasing method' is the alternative.

question: What is added to an FM speech channel to boost the higher audio frequencies?
explanation: Pre-emphasis boosts the higher audio frequencies before modulation. After FM demodulation, noise is strongest at high audio frequencies, so the receiver's matching de-emphasis cuts them back, reducing the noise along with them. The net result is a flat audio response with a better signal-to-noise ratio.

question: Why is de-emphasis used in FM communications receivers?
choices: For compatibility with transmitters using phase modulation
explanation: De-emphasis cuts high audio frequencies in the receiver by 6 dB per octave, the reverse of pre-emphasis. Phase modulation inherently boosts high audio frequencies (PM deviation increases with audio frequency), so de-emphasis makes an FM receiver compatible with PM transmitters and restores a flat audio response.

question: What is meant by the term “baseband” in radio communications?
choices: The lowest frequency band that the transmitter or receiver covers
The frequency range occupied by a message signal prior to modulation
The unmodulated bandwidth of the transmitted signal
The basic oscillator frequency in an FM transmitter that is multiplied to increase the deviation and carrier frequency
explanation: Baseband is the frequency range occupied by the message signal before it modulates a carrier, for example 300-3000 Hz for voice or the bit stream for data. After modulation, the information is moved up to RF around the carrier frequency.

question: What are the principal frequencies that appear at the output of a mixer?
choices: Two and four times the input frequency
The square root of the product of input frequencies
The two input frequencies along with their sum and difference frequencies
explanation: A mixer multiplies two signals. Its output contains the two original input frequencies plus their sum and difference: mixing 14.2 MHz with a 23.2 MHz oscillator gives 9.0 MHz (difference) and 37.4 MHz (sum). A filter then selects the one you want, typically the IF. Real mixers also produce weaker products at harmonic combinations.

question: What occurs when the input signal levels to a mixer are too high?
choices: Excessive AGC voltage levels are generated
explanation: If a mixer's input signals are too strong, it operates nonlinearly and generates spurious products: mixing products of harmonics of the inputs (2f1 − f2, 3f1 − 2f2, and so on) that appear as false signals. Keeping input levels within the mixer's rating keeps it linear.

question: How does a diode envelope detector function?
choices: By rectification and filtering of RF signals
By breakdown of the Zener voltage
By mixing signals with noise in the transition region of the diode
By sensing the change of reactance in the diode with respect to frequency
explanation: A diode envelope detector rectifies the RF signal (the diode passes only one half of each RF cycle) and then filters out the RF with a capacitor, leaving a voltage that follows the peaks of the RF: the envelope. For AM, the envelope is the original audio.

question: Which type of detector is used for demodulating SSB signals?
explanation: A product detector mixes the incoming SSB signal with a signal from a local oscillator (BFO or carrier oscillator) that replaces the carrier suppressed at the transmitter. The difference product is the original audio. An envelope detector can't demodulate SSB because there's no carrier to create a proper envelope.

question: What is meant by “direct sampling” in software defined radios?
choices: Software is converted from source code to object code during operation of the receiver
I and Q signals are generated by digital processing without the use of RF amplification
Incoming RF is digitized by an analog-to-digital converter without being mixed with a local oscillator signal
A switching mixer is used to generate I and Q signals directly from the RF input
explanation: In a direct-sampling SDR, the RF from the antenna (after filtering and perhaps amplification) goes straight into a very fast analog-to-digital converter, with no mixing to an IF. All further processing (tuning, filtering, demodulation) is done digitally. The ADC sample rate must be more than twice the highest frequency received.

question: What kind of digital signal processing audio filter is used to remove unwanted noise from a received SSB signal?
explanation: An adaptive filter continuously adjusts its own coefficients based on the incoming signal. For noise reduction it learns what is correlated (speech, which repeats predictably) and what is random (noise), and suppresses the random part. A crystal-lattice filter is analog, and a Hilbert filter is used to generate SSB.

question: What type of digital signal processing filter is used to generate an SSB signal?
explanation: A Hilbert-transform filter shifts all frequency components of a signal by 90°, regardless of frequency. That's what the DSP phasing method of SSB generation needs: two versions of the audio 90° apart, combined with two carriers 90° apart, so one sideband cancels and the other adds.

question: Which method generates an SSB signal using digital signal processing?
choices: Mixing products are converted to voltages and subtracted by adder circuits
A frequency synthesizer removes unwanted sidebands
Varying quartz crystal characteristics are emulated in digital form
Signals are combined in quadrature phase relationship
explanation: DSP generates SSB with the phasing method: the audio and the carrier are each split into two paths 90° apart (in quadrature), mixed, and then added. The unwanted sideband cancels and the desired sideband reinforces. Choosing to add or subtract the two paths selects USB or LSB.

question: How frequently must an analog signal be sampled to be accurately reproduced?
choices: At least half the rate of the highest frequency component of the signal
At least twice the rate of the highest frequency component of the signal
At the same rate as the highest frequency component of the signal
At four times the rate of the highest frequency component of the signal
explanation: The Nyquist theorem: a signal must be sampled at least twice as fast as its highest frequency component to be reproduced accurately. A 3 kHz audio signal needs at least 6 kHz sampling (in practice 8 kHz or more). Anything above half the sample rate gets aliased into false lower frequencies.

question: What is the minimum number of bits required to sample a signal with a range of 1 volt at a resolution of 1 millivolt?
explanation: A 1 V range at 1 mV resolution needs 1 V / 1 mV = 1000 different levels. The number of levels is 2 to the power of the number of bits: 2^9 = 512 is not enough, 2^10 = 1024 is. So at least 10 bits are needed.

question: What function is performed by a Fast Fourier Transform?
choices: Converting analog signals to digital form
Converting digital signals to analog form
Converting signals from the time domain to the frequency domain
Converting signals from the frequency domain to the time domain
explanation: A Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) converts a signal from the time domain (amplitude vs. time) to the frequency domain (amplitude vs. frequency). It's how an SDR produces its spectrum and waterfall display. The inverse FFT goes the other way.

question: What is the function of decimation?
choices: Converting data to binary-coded decimal form
Reducing the effective sample rate by removing samples
explanation: Decimation reduces the sample rate by keeping only every Nth sample (decimation by N). After a signal has been narrowed by filtering, a lower sample rate is enough, and processing it requires much less computing power. It must be preceded by a low-pass filter to prevent aliasing.

question: Why is an anti-aliasing filter required in a decimator?
choices: It removes high-frequency signal components that would otherwise be reproduced as lower frequency components
It peaks the response of the decimator, improving bandwidth
It removes low-frequency signal components to eliminate the need for DC restoration
It notches out the sampling frequency to avoid sampling errors
explanation: When the sample rate is reduced, the new Nyquist frequency (half the new rate) is lower. Any signal components above it would alias, folding down to appear as false lower-frequency signals. The anti-aliasing filter removes them before decimation.

question: What aspect of receiver analog-to-digital conversion determines the maximum receive bandwidth of a direct-sampling software defined radio (SDR)?
explanation: A direct-sampling SDR can digitize frequencies up to half its sample rate (the Nyquist limit), so the sample rate determines the maximum receive bandwidth. A 122.88 MHz ADC can see everything from DC to about 61 MHz at once. The number of bits affects dynamic range, not bandwidth.

question: What sets the minimum detectable signal level for a direct-sampling software defined receiver in the absence of atmospheric or thermal noise?
choices: Reference voltage level and sample width in bits
explanation: An ADC's smallest step is its reference voltage divided by 2^n (n = number of bits). A signal smaller than about one step can't be represented, and the rounding errors create quantization noise. So the reference voltage and the sample width in bits set the minimum detectable signal, and each extra bit improves it by about 6 dB.

question: Which of the following is generally true of Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filters?
choices: FIR filters can delay all frequency components of the signal by the same amount
FIR filters are easier to implement for a given set of passband rolloff requirements
FIR filters can respond faster to impulses
explanation: An FIR filter can be designed with linear phase: every frequency component is delayed by the same amount of time. The waveform shape is preserved, which matters for data signals and avoids the ringing and distortion caused by phase shifts in analog and IIR filters. The trade-off is that FIR filters need many taps (more computation).

question: What is the function of taps in a digital signal processing filter?
choices: To reduce excess signal pressure levels
Select the point at which baseband signals are generated
Provide incremental signal delays for filter algorithms
explanation: A digital filter keeps a chain of recent samples, each delayed by one sample period: each point in the chain is a 'tap'. Each tap is multiplied by a coefficient, and the results are added to form the output. The taps provide the incremental delays the filter algorithm needs.

question: Which of the following would allow a digital signal processing filter to create a sharper filter response?
explanation: More taps means the filter looks at a longer stretch of signal, which allows a sharper transition between passband and stopband (steeper skirts) and deeper rejection. The cost is more computation and more delay (latency).

question: What is the typical output impedance of an op-amp?
explanation: An op-amp's output impedance is very low (ideally zero, in practice a few ohms or less with feedback). It can drive loads without its output voltage changing much.

question: What is the frequency response of the circuit in E7-3 if a capacitor is added across the feedback resistor?
explanation: A capacitor across RF lowers the feedback impedance as frequency rises (XC = 1 / 2πfC). Since gain = feedback impedance / R1, the gain falls at high frequencies, making the circuit a low-pass filter (an active integrator). The corner frequency is where XC equals RF.

question: What is the typical input impedance of an op-amp?
explanation: An op-amp's input impedance is very high (ideally infinite; megohms for bipolar-input types and far more for FET-input types). The inputs draw almost no current, so they don't load the source.

question: What is meant by the term “op-amp input offset voltage”?
choices: The output voltage of the op-amp minus its input voltage
The difference between the output voltage of the op-amp and the input voltage required in the immediately following stage
The differential input voltage needed to bring the open loop output voltage to zero
The potential between the amplifier input terminals of the op-amp in an open loop condition
explanation: Because of tiny mismatches between the transistors inside, a real op-amp's output isn't exactly zero with both inputs at the same voltage. The input offset voltage is the small differential voltage (typically microvolts to a few millivolts) that must be applied between the inputs to bring the open-loop output to zero.

question: How can unwanted ringing and audio instability be prevented in an op-amp audio filter?
explanation: High gain and high Q make an active filter prone to ringing (a damped oscillation after each sound) and even continuous oscillation. Limiting both the gain and the Q of each stage keeps the filter stable. For a narrower response, cascade several low-Q stages instead of using one high-Q stage.

question: What is the gain-bandwidth of an operational amplifier?
choices: The maximum frequency for a filter circuit using that type of amplifier
The frequency at which the open-loop gain of the amplifier equals one
The gain of the amplifier at a filter’s cutoff frequency
The frequency at which the amplifier’s offset voltage is zero
explanation: An op-amp's open-loop gain falls with frequency. The gain-bandwidth product is the frequency at which the open-loop gain has dropped to 1 (unity), and it's constant: an op-amp with 1 MHz gain-bandwidth can give a gain of 100 up to 10 kHz, or 10 up to 100 kHz.

question: What voltage gain can be expected from the circuit in Figure E7-3 when R1 is 10 ohms and RF is 470 ohms?
explanation: Figure E7-3 is an inverting amplifier with gain = −RF / R1. Magnitude: 470 / 10 = 47. The minus sign just indicates the output is inverted (180° out of phase).

question: How does the gain of an ideal operational amplifier vary with frequency?
choices: It increases linearly with increasing frequency
It decreases linearly with increasing frequency
It decreases logarithmically with increasing frequency
It does not vary with frequency
explanation: An ideal op-amp is assumed to have infinite gain at all frequencies, so its gain does not vary with frequency. Real op-amps lose gain at higher frequencies (see gain-bandwidth product).

question: What will be the output voltage of the circuit shown in Figure E7-3 if R1 is 1,000 ohms, RF is 10,000 ohms, and 0.23 volts DC is applied to the input?
explanation: Inverting amplifier: Vout = −(RF / R1) × Vin = −(10,000 / 1,000) × 0.23 V = −10 × 0.23 = −2.3 V. The gain is 10, and the output is inverted, so a positive input gives a negative output.

question: What absolute voltage gain can be expected from the circuit in Figure E7-3 when R1 is 1,800 ohms and RF is 68 kilohms?
explanation: Gain = RF / R1 = 68,000 / 1,800 ≈ 37.8, so about 38. (The absolute value ignores the minus sign for inversion.)

question: What absolute voltage gain can be expected from the circuit in Figure E7-3 when R1 is 3,300 ohms and RF is 47 kilohms?
What is an operational amplifier?
choices: A high-gain, direct-coupled differential amplifier with very high input impedance and very low output impedance
A digital audio amplifier whose characteristics are determined by components external to the amplifier
An amplifier used to increase the average output of frequency modulated amateur signals to the legal limit
A RF amplifier used in the UHF and microwave regions
explanation: An op-amp is a high-gain, direct-coupled (works down to DC) differential amplifier with very high input impedance and very low output impedance. Its behavior in a circuit is set almost entirely by the external feedback components.

question: What are three common oscillator circuits?
explanation: Colpitts, Hartley and Pierce are three classic oscillator circuits. A Colpitts gets feedback from a capacitive divider, a Hartley from a tapped coil, and a Pierce through a quartz crystal. The other names in the distractors are made up.

question: What is a microphonic?
choices: An IC used for amplifying microphone signals
Distortion caused by RF pickup on the microphone cable
Changes in oscillator frequency caused by mechanical vibration
Excess loading of the microphone by an oscillator
explanation: A 'microphonic' is an unwanted change in an oscillator's frequency caused by mechanical vibration: shaking or tapping moves coils, capacitor plates or the circuit board slightly, which changes their inductance or capacitance. The result can be a warbling signal when a speaker, fan or footsteps shake the radio.

question: What is a phase-locked loop?
choices: An electronic servo loop consisting of a ratio detector, reactance modulator, and voltage-controlled oscillator
An electronic circuit also known as a monostable multivibrator
An electronic servo loop consisting of a phase detector, a low-pass filter, a voltage-controlled oscillator, and a stable reference oscillator
An electronic circuit consisting of a precision push-pull amplifier with a differential phase input
explanation: A phase-locked loop is a feedback (servo) loop: a phase detector compares the VCO's output with a stable reference oscillator, the low-pass filter smooths the phase detector's error voltage, and that voltage steers the voltage-controlled oscillator until it's locked in phase with the reference.

question: How is positive feedback supplied in a Colpitts oscillator?
explanation: A Colpitts oscillator takes its positive feedback from a capacitive voltage divider across the tank circuit (two capacitors in series). A tapped coil provides feedback in a Hartley oscillator. Memory aid: Colpitts = Capacitors.

question: How is positive feedback supplied in a Pierce oscillator?
explanation: In a Pierce oscillator the quartz crystal itself is in the feedback path, between the output and input of the amplifier (usually with capacitors to ground on each side). The crystal only passes feedback efficiently at its resonant frequency, so it sets the frequency very precisely.

question: Which of these functions can be performed by a phase-locked loop?
choices: Wide-band AF and RF power amplification
Comparison of two digital input signals and digital pulse counting
explanation: PLLs are used for frequency synthesis (a divider between the VCO and phase detector makes the VCO run at N times the reference, giving many precise frequencies) and FM demodulation (the VCO control voltage follows the incoming signal's frequency changes, which is the audio).

question: How can an oscillator’s microphonic responses be reduced?
choices: Reduce noise on the oscillator’s power supply
Mechanically isolate the oscillator circuitry from its enclosure
explanation: Microphonics are caused by vibration, so the cure is mechanical: rigidly mount the oscillator components, and isolate the oscillator circuitry from the enclosure, for example with shock mounts or rubber grommets, so vibration isn't transmitted to it.

question: Which of the following components can be used to reduce thermal drift in crystal oscillators?
explanation: NP0 (also called C0G) ceramic capacitors have nearly zero temperature coefficient: their capacitance barely changes with temperature. Using them in oscillator circuits prevents the frequency from drifting as the equipment warms up.

question: What type of frequency synthesizer circuit uses a phase accumulator, lookup table, digital-to-analog converter, and a low-pass anti-alias filter?
explanation: A direct digital synthesizer (DDS) works like this: a phase accumulator adds a frequency value to a running total each clock cycle; that phase addresses a lookup table of waveform amplitude values (a sine wave); a DAC turns the numbers into a voltage; and a low-pass filter removes sampling artifacts. The step size sets the output frequency.

question: What information is contained in the lookup table of a direct digital synthesizer (DDS)?
choices: The phase relationship between a reference oscillator and the output waveform
Amplitude values that represent the desired waveform
The phase relationship between a voltage-controlled oscillator and the output waveform
Frequently used receiver and transmitter frequencies
explanation: The DDS lookup table holds amplitude values of one cycle of the desired waveform (usually a sine wave). The phase accumulator output is used as an address, and the table returns the amplitude for that point in the cycle.

question: What are the major spectral impurity components of direct digital synthesizers?
explanation: A DDS creates its waveform from a limited number of samples and bits, so rounding errors repeat in patterns. These produce spurious signals at discrete frequencies (spurs), rather than broadband noise. A low-pass filter and careful frequency planning minimize them.

question: Which of the following ensures that a crystal oscillator operates on the frequency specified by the crystal manufacturer?
choices: Provide the crystal with a specified parallel inductance
Provide the crystal with a specified parallel capacitance
Bias the crystal at a specified voltage
Bias the crystal at a specified current
explanation: A parallel-mode crystal is calibrated to oscillate at its marked frequency with a specified load capacitance in parallel with it (e.g., 20 pF or 32 pF). Provide a different capacitance and the frequency will be slightly off. Series-mode crystals are calibrated with no load capacitance.

question: Which of the following is a technique for providing highly accurate and stable oscillators needed for microwave transmission and reception?
choices: Use a rubidium stabilized reference oscillator
Use a temperature-controlled high Q dielectric resonator
explanation: All three are used for accurate, stable microwave oscillators: locking to a GPS-disciplined reference (accurate to parts per billion), using a rubidium atomic reference oscillator, or using a temperature-controlled, high-Q dielectric resonator oscillator. Microwave frequencies multiply any reference error, so the reference must be very stable.

question: What technique shows that a square wave is made up of a sine wave and its odd harmonics?
explanation: Fourier analysis shows that any periodic waveform can be built from sine waves: the fundamental plus harmonics. A square wave consists of the fundamental and its odd harmonics (3rd, 5th, 7th...), with amplitudes of 1/3, 1/5, 1/7... of the fundamental. Adding more harmonics makes the edges sharper.

question: Which of the following is a type of analog-to-digital conversion?
explanation: Successive approximation is a common ADC method. It compares the input to the output of an internal DAC, testing one bit at a time from the most significant bit down: 'is the input above half scale? above three quarters?' and so on. An n-bit conversion takes n steps.

question: Which of the following describes a signal in the time domain?
explanation: A time-domain display shows amplitude at different times, like an oscilloscope. A frequency-domain display (spectrum analyzer) shows amplitude at different frequencies. The FFT converts between the two.

question: What is “dither” with respect to analog-to-digital converters?
choices: An abnormal condition where the converter cannot settle on a value to represent the signal
A small amount of noise added to the input signal to reduce quantization noise
An error caused by irregular quantization step size
A method of decimation by randomly skipping samples
explanation: Dither is a small amount of random noise deliberately added to an ADC's input. Without it, signals near the size of one quantization step produce distortion products that are correlated with the signal. The noise randomizes the quantization errors, turning distortion into a slightly higher but uniform noise floor, which improves the effective resolution.

question: What is the benefit of making voltage measurements with a true-RMS calculating meter?
choices: An inverse Fourier transform can be used
The signal’s RMS noise factor is also calculated
The calculated RMS value can be converted directly into phasor form
RMS is measured for both sinusoidal and non-sinusoidal signals
explanation: A true-RMS meter calculates the actual RMS (heating) value of any waveform. Simpler meters measure the average or peak and scale it assuming a sine wave, so they read incorrectly on square waves, SSB, noise or distorted waveforms. True-RMS reads correctly for both sinusoidal and non-sinusoidal signals.

question: What is the approximate ratio of PEP-to-average power in an unprocessed single-sideband phone signal?
explanation: Unprocessed voice has high peaks and much lower average level, so an SSB signal's PEP is typically about 2.5 times its average power (a peak-to-average ratio of about 4 dB). Speech processing raises the average power closer to the peak.

question: What determines the PEP-to-average power ratio of an unprocessed single-sideband phone signal?
choices: The frequency of the modulating signal
explanation: An SSB signal's envelope follows the voice waveform, so its PEP-to-average ratio depends on the speech characteristics: how the voice's peaks relate to its average level, which varies between speakers and languages. The other choices don't affect the envelope shape.

question: Why are direct or flash conversion analog-to-digital converters used for a software defined radio?
choices: Very low power consumption decreases frequency drift
Immunity to out-of-sequence coding reduces spurious responses
Very high speed allows digitizing high frequencies
explanation: A flash ADC uses a separate comparator for each quantization level and converts in a single step, making it the fastest type of converter. That very high speed makes it possible to digitize high frequencies directly in an SDR. The trade-off is high power consumption and complexity.

question: How many different input levels can be encoded by an analog-to-digital converter with 8-bit resolution?
choices: 8 multiplied by the gain of the input amplifier
256 divided by the gain of the input amplifier
explanation: An ADC with n bits can encode 2^n different levels: 2^8 = 256 for 8 bits. Each extra bit doubles the number of levels and adds about 6 dB of dynamic range.

question: What is the purpose of a low-pass filter used at the output of a digital-to-analog converter?
choices: Lower the input bandwidth to increase the effective resolution
Improve accuracy by removing out-of-sequence codes from the input
Remove spurious sampling artifacts from the output signal
explanation: A DAC outputs a staircase waveform that contains the desired signal plus images around multiples of the sample rate. A low-pass (reconstruction) filter at the output removes these sampling artifacts, leaving a smooth analog signal.

question: Which of the following is a measure of the quality of an analog-to-digital converter?
explanation: Total harmonic distortion (THD) measures how much an ADC adds harmonics to a pure input signal, reflecting its linearity. Other ADC quality measures include signal-to-noise ratio, spurious-free dynamic range and effective number of bits (ENOB).

question: What is the modulation index of an FM signal?
choices: The ratio of frequency deviation to modulating signal frequency
The ratio of modulating signal amplitude to frequency deviation
The modulating signal frequency divided by the bandwidth of the transmitted signal
The bandwidth of the transmitted signal divided by the modulating signal frequency
explanation: FM modulation index = frequency deviation ÷ modulating frequency. With 3 kHz deviation and 1 kHz audio, the index is 3. It varies with the audio frequency; the deviation ratio is the same calculation at the maximum deviation and highest audio frequency.

question: How does the modulation index of a phase-modulated emission vary with RF carrier frequency?
choices: It increases as the RF carrier frequency increases
It decreases as the RF carrier frequency increases
It varies with the square root of the RF carrier frequency
It does not depend on the RF carrier frequency
explanation: For phase modulation, the modulation index is the peak phase shift (in radians) produced by the modulator. It depends only on the modulating signal's amplitude, not on the RF carrier frequency. (With PM, frequency deviation rises with audio frequency, but the phase index doesn't change with the carrier frequency.)

question: What is the modulation index of an FM phone signal having a maximum frequency deviation of 3000 Hz either side of the carrier frequency if the highest modulating frequency is 1000 Hz?
explanation: Modulation index = deviation ÷ modulating frequency = 3000 Hz ÷ 1000 Hz = 3.

question: What is the modulation index of an FM phone signal having a maximum carrier deviation of plus or minus 6 kHz if the highest modulating frequency  is 2 kHz?
explanation: Modulation index = deviation ÷ modulating frequency = 6 kHz ÷ 2 kHz = 3.

question: What is the deviation ratio of an FM phone signal having a maximum frequency swing of plus or minus 5 kHz if the highest modulation frequency is 3 kHz?
explanation: Deviation ratio = maximum deviation ÷ highest modulating frequency = 5 kHz ÷ 3 kHz = 1.67. This is the standard for 'wideband' amateur FM with 5 kHz deviation.

question: What is the deviation ratio of an FM phone signal having a maximum frequency swing of plus or minus 7.5 kHz if the highest modulation frequency is 3.5 kHz?
explanation: Deviation ratio = maximum deviation ÷ highest modulating frequency = 7.5 kHz ÷ 3.5 kHz = 2.14.

question: Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) is a technique used for which types of amateur communication?
choices: OFDM signals are not allowed on amateur bands
explanation: OFDM is used for digital modes in amateur radio, for example in VARA, some Winlink modes, digital voice (FreeDV) and DVB-T amateur television. It's robust against multipath and selective fading.

question: What describes orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM)?
choices: A frequency modulation technique that uses non-harmonically related frequencies
A bandwidth compression technique using Fourier transforms
A digital mode for narrow-band, slow-speed transmissions
A digital modulation technique using subcarriers at frequencies chosen to avoid intersymbol interference
explanation: OFDM divides the data among many closely spaced subcarriers, each modulated at a slow symbol rate. The subcarrier spacing is chosen so the subcarriers are mathematically orthogonal: each one has its peak where all the others are zero, so they don't interfere, even though their spectra overlap. The slow symbol rate avoids intersymbol interference from multipath.

question: What is deviation ratio?
choices: The ratio of the audio modulating frequency to the center carrier frequency
The ratio of the maximum carrier frequency deviation to the highest audio modulating frequency
The ratio of the carrier center frequency to the audio modulating frequency
The ratio of the highest audio modulating frequency to the average audio modulating frequency
explanation: Deviation ratio = maximum carrier frequency deviation ÷ highest audio modulating frequency. It's the 'worst-case' modulation index of a system; for amateur FM, 5 kHz ÷ 3 kHz = 1.67.

question: What is frequency division multiplexing (FDM)?
choices: The transmitted signal jumps from band to band at a predetermined rate
Dividing the transmitted signal into separate frequency bands that each carry a different data stream
The transmitted signal is divided into packets of information
Two or more information streams are merged into a digital combiner, which then pulse position modulates the transmitter
explanation: Frequency division multiplexing divides the available spectrum into separate frequency bands (subchannels), each carrying its own data stream at the same time. Old telephone carrier systems and broadcast radio are examples.

question: What is digital time division multiplexing?
choices: Two or more data streams are assigned to discrete sub-carriers on an FM transmitter
Two or more signals are arranged to share discrete time slots of a data transmission
Two or more data streams share the same channel by transmitting time of transmission as the sub-carrier
Two or more signals are quadrature modulated to increase bandwidth efficiency
explanation: Time division multiplexing gives each signal its own time slot: signals take turns using the full channel, cycling quickly through the slots. DMR digital radio, for example, uses two time slots so one repeater carries two conversations at once.

question: What is Quadrature Amplitude Modulation or QAM?
choices: A technique for digital data compression used in digital television which removes redundancy in the data by comparing bit amplitudes
Transmission of data by modulating the amplitude of two carriers of the same frequency but 90 degrees out of phase
A method of performing single sideband modulation by shifting the phase of the carrier and modulation components of the signal
A technique for analog modulation of television video signals using phase modulation and compression
explanation: QAM modulates the amplitude of two carriers at the same frequency but 90° apart in phase (the I and Q carriers). Combining them gives each symbol a specific amplitude and phase. 16-QAM has 16 possible combinations, carrying 4 bits per symbol.

question: What is the definition of symbol rate in a digital transmission?
choices: The number of control characters in a message packet
The maximum rate at which the forward error correction code can make corrections
The rate at which the waveform changes to convey information
The number of characters carried per second by the station-to-station link
explanation: Symbol rate is the rate at which the transmitted waveform changes to convey information (symbols per second, or baud). If each symbol represents multiple bits (e.g., 4 bits in 16-QAM), the bit rate is higher than the symbol rate.
